item.title: I stopped trusting Google and Microsoft with my notes after switching to this open-source app
item.itunes:title: I stopped trusting Google and Microsoft with my notes after switching to this open-source app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've tried plenty of note-taking apps, but managing my notes shouldn't mean jumping between different tools or giving up control over my data. I wanted something flexible enough for everyday use without being tied to a single company's ecosystem. That's what led me to Joplin, an open-source note-taking app that takes a different approach to managing personal information. It offers a practical way to handle my notes while giving me more freedom over how I use and store them. After spending time with it, I can see why it deserves a place in my daily workflow.

Joplin is more than just a place to store notes

A simpler way to capture every thought

Joplin works well for different note-taking needs without making the experience complicated. Some days, I need a place to jot down a quick idea. Other times, I want to keep detailed research notes or document something I've been working on. Joplin handles these different needs in one application.

I can create separate notebooks for different areas of my life and keep related information together. This makes my collection easier to navigate as it grows instead of leaving me with a long list of unrelated notes.

Another thing I appreciate is that Joplin doesn't try to be an all-in-one productivity suite. Its main focus is note-taking, and I don't need to build an elaborate system before I can start using it. I can keep my setup simple and add more structure whenever I need it.

This flexibility makes Joplin useful for both everyday notes and information I want to keep for the long term, without adding unnecessary complexity to my workflow.

Markdown and organization make managing notes effortless

Keeping my notes organized without overthinking

Joplin gives me enough flexibility to organize my notes without spending too much time managing them. I can use notebooks to group related information and add tags when a note belongs to multiple topics. This makes it easier to maintain a consistent structure as my collection grows.

Markdown is another useful part of this setup. It keeps formatting simple and makes notes easier to read, while Joplin's editor lets me work without relying on Markdown syntax all the time. I can choose whichever approach feels more convenient for the task.

I also appreciate having control over how detailed my organization system becomes. I don't need to create multiple layers of folders or follow a strict structure from day one. I can start with a few notebooks and refine them as my needs change.

When I need to revisit something, I can combine my existing organization with Joplin's search and filtering options to narrow down the results. This approach keeps note management practical. Instead of constantly reorganizing information, I can spend more time using it.

5 Joplin plugins you need to use to improve your note-taking

Take better looking, more useful notes

By  Patrick Hearn

Self-hosted sync gives me control over my notes

My notes sync on my terms

One of the biggest reasons I chose Joplin is its flexible synchronization system. I can sync my notes across devices without relying entirely on a third-party service. Joplin supports several synchronization options, including Joplin Server, which I can host on my own infrastructure.

Setting up Joplin Server gives me more control over where my notes are synchronized and stored. I can access my information across supported devices while keeping the synchronization service under my control. This fits well with my preference for self-hosted tools that let me manage my own data.

However, self-hosting also comes with some responsibility. I need to keep the server updated, maintain reliable backups, and make sure my setup continues to work properly. It's not a completely maintenance-free solution, but the additional control makes the effort worthwhile for my needs.

I also like that self-hosting isn't mandatory. Joplin supports other synchronization methods, so users can choose an option that matches their technical skills and preferences. This flexibility makes it easier to get started without committing to running a server.

The little features that make Joplin useful every day

More convenience, fewer extra apps

Beyond its core note-taking features, Joplin includes several useful tools that make my daily workflow easier. The built-in to-do feature lets me create checklists and manage simple tasks without opening another app. I can keep these alongside my notes, which is convenient when I want to track small tasks related to something I'm working on. I love the split-screen editor; it completely changes how I write.

The Web Clipper is another feature worth mentioning. It lets me save web pages and selected content directly to Joplin through a browser extension. I find this useful when collecting information from the web that I might want to revisit later. Instead of relying on bookmarks alone, I can keep useful content available in my notes.

Joplin also supports plugins, so I can extend its functionality when the built-in features aren't enough. The available options make it possible to customize the app around my preferences rather than settling for a fixed set of features.

None of these additions feels essential on its own, but together they make Joplin more versatile. I can keep my everyday information and supporting resources in one place without turning my note-taking setup into a complicated productivity system.

7 Joplin power-user features you didn't know existed

Joplin is more capable than you think

1
By  Parth Shah

Fewer apps, more control over my notes

Joplin has earned its place in my setup by making note-taking feel simple without taking control away from me. It may not have the polished interface of some commercial alternatives, but it gets the important things right. I can keep my information organized, choose how I sync it, and build a workflow that suits my needs.

Joplin

Joplin is an open-source note-taking app and a great competitor to Microsoft's OneNote and Google Keep.

item.title: One of the first public Switch 2 emulators is already running Mario Kart World shockingly well
item.itunes:title: One of the first public Switch 2 emulators is already running Mario Kart World shockingly well
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Experimental Switch 2 emulator Eglantine runs Mario Kart World at decent/full speed on powerful PCs.
  • Eglantine is FOSS and derived from Eden/Yuzu/Sudachi.
  • Switch 2 emulation is moving extremely fast following the recent release of a jailbreak.

It's been a wild few weeks in the gaming world. We've seen several AI-assisted Switch PC ports land, including Zelda: Link's Awakening and the Pokémon: Let's Go games, along with a tool called Nxnative that lets Switch games run directly on Mac. While clips of Mario Kart World running on Mac and PC have been floating around the internet for the past few days, an emulator for Nintendo's Switch 2 hasn't dropped publicly — at least until now.

First, modder Takoroka released an experimental Switch 2 integration for Switch emulator Eden called NX2. Takoroka says their Switch 2 version of Eden is still a work in progress and needs a lot more work. That said, it laid the groundwork for Eglantine, a fork of NX2 and the emulator that seems to run Mario Kart World best right now. While Eglantine seems to be the most capable Switch 2 PC emulator currently (as long as you have a powerful gaming PC), several other similar projects are also in development.

The emulator is described as "very experimental," but its compatibility description says it's capable of "running Mario Kart World at decent/full speed depending on specs and configuration." There are also reports that Splatoon Raiders boots, though at a low frame rate. Of course, to use an emulator like Eglantine, you need a compatible Mario Kart World file, which you'd need to dump from your legally obtained copy of the game. Like similar projects, Eglantine's development is heavily AI-assisted.

"Eglantine is a free and open-source (FOSS) Switch 2 emulator, derived from Eden, Yuzu and Sudachi — started by developer Camille LaVey. It's written in C++ with portability in mind, with builds for Windows, Linux and macOS," reads the project's GitHub page.

This is likely a good sign for the future of Switch 2 emulation

We'll likely see game compatibility improve at a rapid rate

In a clip shared on YouTube from Techno Ninja (check it out above), Mario Kart World seems to run reasonably well in Eglantine. There are a few stutters, but there aren't any major graphical glitches, and the overall experience seems like a notable step up from what we saw a few days ago.

Splatoon Raiders runs far more poorly, and the entire game seems to crash toward the end of the clip shared by YouTuber ewnicky, but it doesn't seem to boot in Eglantine. Still, the fact that one game is already pretty playable and another boots up is encouraging given the Switch 2 was just jailbroken a little over a week ago.

In other AI port-related news, Anthropic seems to have introduced an instruction telling Claude not to recreate specific existing games, even if they're renamed, potentially limiting the explosive growth the retro and modern PC port space has seen over the past few weeks.

Anthropic seems to be testing a potential crackdown on vibe-coded ports of existing games

It's unclear if the AI giant is just A/B testing a potential new guardrail or if it will be more widely implemented.

By  Adam Conway

item.title: Running Windows apps on Linux just changed forever, and I was one of the first to try it
item.itunes:title: Running Windows apps on Linux just changed forever, and I was one of the first to try it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Being able to replace Windows with Linux has been the dream of many, including myself, for a long time. But software compatibility has always been the biggest hurdle. The Wine compatibility layer is great, but it won't make the latest version of Photoshop or Microsoft Office run on your PC, and virtualization without GPU passthrough just isn't suitable for demanding apps like Photoshop.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That's changing now thanks to LSW — a project developed by a close friend of mine. I've been extremely excited about this since before it went public, and now that it's available for anyone to try, I can finally talk about it.

Why is LSW so great?

Windows on Linux is a mess

LSW requires some context to fully comprehend why it's so great. Windows apps don't run natively on Linux, and whether it's because of the smaller market share or any other reason, many popular apps don't make their way to Linux users in a native package. This leaves a big gap in the software that is available for the platform, and so far, there have been a couple of ways to address that.

Wine is a big one, and while it works great for games and some older software, too many modern pieces of software simply don't work through Wine. You won't be able to install Photoshop or Microsoft Office just using Wine, and some apps that can technically function require a lot of prep work. That's why projects like Affinity for Linux come with dedicated installers to set everything up correctly, though even then, it can be glitchy.

The other option is virtualization, but that has its own hurdles. Most virtualization solutions to run Windows on Linux — such as WinBoat — support no hardware acceleration on the guest operating system, so the entire experience runs in software mode. It works, but things aren't as performant as you'd expect, and then apps that require hardware acceleration, such as Photoshop, simply don't work.

I tried Winpodx, WinBoat, and WinApps for running Windows software on Linux, and one is clearly ahead

An easy decision

2
By  João Carrasqueira

This is a problem that's tried to be addressed by Looking Glass, a solution that enables GPU passthrough for Windows virtual machines so you can make use of your hardware to get better performance. The problem with this solution is that GPU passthrough means the GPU assigned to your virtual machine is essentially disconnected from the host operating system, so you can only use it with one or the other at any given time, and changing that requires some work each time. It also doesn't work for every machine, as many laptops don't allow you to pass through a discrete GPU to the VM.

LSW changes everything

LSW finally makes things frictionless thanks to GPU paravirtualization. Using dedicated drivers on the guest OS, your Windows VM is able to pass instructions along to the GPU on your host operating system, supporting hardware acceleration on essentially any hardware (as long as it's x86, that is) and without any complicated setup. It allows your Windows VM to run smoothly, and it means more demanding Windows apps can finally run on Linux in a usable way.

I've been using LSW daily for weeks to work with Affinity, and it's an absolute game changer. The initial release only worked well on my PCs with AMD integrated GPUs, but as I passed that feedback to the developer, there have been some updates, and it now works well with Intel iGPUs and Nvidia discrete GPUs, too.

I tried running Windows apps on Linux with Wine, but virtualization is still better

Wine is for very specific instances

2
By  João Carrasqueira

I should note that even now, LSW is in a very early alpha stage. My friend only has a limited set of hardware he can test his work on, and while I've tried to help him expand the pool of hardware and software to test, there's only so much ground we can realistically cover between the two of us. If you decide to try it, there are still bound to be plenty of issues.

Currently, a pre-built binary of LSW is only available through the Arch User Repository (AUR). If you have Arch or one of its derivatives along with an AUR helper, you'll want to install the package called lsw-bin.

Setting up LSW

Simple and fast

As much as I want to talk about the experience of using Windows itself, there's more to LSW that makes it great because it's very easy to set up while also being generally fast. While I quite liked WinBoat's visual design, I always noted that it felt more like a web app, and that's because it kind of is. The WinBoat manager uses Electron, which is famously resource-hungry and doesn't feel native on any platform.

LSW uses Qt for its UI framework, so it fits right in with my KDE Plasma desktop, and it feels smoother and lighter to use, too. The initial setup is relatively easy. You provide your own Windows ISO (there's a download option, but it's not currently functional), and then you have the option to trim the Windows image. It should be noted that I had issues using an older Windows ISO, so I recommend using Windows 11 version 26H2 for this, as well as sticking to the US English ISO.

Trimming removes unnecessary editions from the multi-edition ISO, plus it removes a lot of pre-installed apps, while leaving some essentials like Windows Update, WebView2, and other generally important Windows features. There's also a more extreme trimming option that removes these features as well, making Windows even smaller, but potentially breaking some features.

I debloated Windows 11 without breaking anything, and here's what I deliberately left alone

How much do you trust the debloater you got from GitHub?

1
By  Abhinav Raj

After that, you can select how many CPU cores to make available to the VM, as well as how much RAM and storage you want the VM to have. CPU resources are allocated as needed, and the disk dynamically expands to the maximum size you set, but the RAM you assign is locked to the VM as long as it's running, meaning that RAM can't be used by the host operating system if the VM is running in any capacity.

You can customize the user account name and password too, but personally, I leave all these options as the default. Then, all you need to do is wait a few minutes while LSW handles the setup process for Windows. It's entirely unattended and creates a local user account in Windows, so there's no Microsoft account requirement. All the driver setup work happens automatically during this stage, so once setup is complete, you can just start using the VM.

But is it actually good?

Yes, yes it is

It hardly even matters

Again, there are bound to be some issues with something so early in development, but the way things are looking on the machines I've been able to try is incredibly exciting. For the first time, I can imagine a world where a Linux PC does everything I need, and that's a huge accomplishment. item.itunes:title: You don't need a Tailscale exit node just to reach devices on your home network
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Tailscale feels like magic when you first start using it. You install it on your phone and desktop, and connecting the two from anywhere feels almost too easy, but when you try and open a web interface for a service hosted on your NAS, or check a home security camera away from home and nothing loads. One of the first fixes that's commonly thrown around is using exit nodes, and while they might work, they're probably not actually what you're looking for.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
I use Tailscale to remotely access my self-hosted services - here's how

Tailscale provides an easy way to access your home server from external networks

9
By  Ayush Pande

Tailscale exit nodes are about internet traffic

Tailscale is an overlay network first

When you first set up Tailscale and add devices, it acts as an overlay network. It connects these devices running Tailscale to each other and leaves everything else alone, meaning your browsing, streaming, and app traffic still goes out whatever internet connection you're on. It's why your phone that's connected to your tailnet can reach the other devices on it but not the printer that isn't apart of that network.

An exit node changes how your internet traffic leaves your device, not necessarily which home devices it can reach. When you use a device as an exit node, your device will send all of its traffic through that machine, so websites and apps will see your home IP address instead of whatever network is actually giving you connection to the internet. In practice it works similarly to a traditional VPN with a server you own, which can absolutely be useful, but it doesn't aim your connection to the devices in your home that aren't part of your tailnet.

Tailscale exit nodes take my home internet with me when I travel

A tool waiting for a use case.

3
By  Shekhar Vaidya

Subnet routing is what you're looking for

Tailscale has this functionality built-in, too

If you're trying to reach devices on your home LAN, subnet routers are the better way to do it. A lot of users mistake the "Allow local network access" toggle for an exit node for a switch that allows them to access their home LAN, but that switch affects the network your device is currently on, like the coffee shop or hotel Wi-Fi.

A subnet router is a device on your tailnet that advertises a range of local addresses—the normal 192.168.x.x type—and forwards traffic to that range for everything else in your tailnet. This lets Tailscale reach devices that don't run Tailscale without changing the way your internet traffic is routed. This is obviously good for devices that you haven't installed Tailscale on, but it's the perfect solution for devices that can't install it at all, like a printer.

Setup only takes a few minutes: you will need a device on your network that will always be on, like a Raspberry Pi or a small Linux VM or LXC. You can run Tailscale on it with the --advertise-routes flag with your home subnet, and then you approve the route in your Tailscale admin console. Windows, macOS, iOS and Android clienets will pick up the new route automatically. For Linux, it needs the --accept-routes flag before it can use the routes other devices advertise.

A small pitfall that's worth looking out for is which local address space your router uses. For most people this will be the standard 192.168.0.x space, but if your home LAN and network your connecting from both use that same space, your device won't be able to tell local addresses from remote ones. If you're setting this up, moving your home network to a less common range does prevent headaches like this later.

Is Tailscale the safest way to access your home network remotely?

Tailscale is easy to set up, but is that trading off your security?

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

item.title: The most useful local AI model I've installed this year doesn't write a single word
item.itunes:title: The most useful local AI model I've installed this year doesn't write a single word
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve tried local LLMs for coding and writing, and they do a decent job when you give them smaller tasks. If you’re developing something, breaking a feature into a few steps gives the model a much better chance of getting it right. I think there’s a lot of useful work these models can do that gets overlooked when we only compare them to cloud models on bigger tasks.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

One of the more useful things I’ve done recently is add Tev1 4B to my n8n workflow to find emails that need a reply. It’s a small decision model that reads a message and checks it against criteria I’ve provided. That sounds like a modest job, but it’s become one of my favorite uses for local AI, and it doesn’t involve writing a single word or generating any code.

My inbox needs more than sender filters

Finding the emails worth replying to

I get a lot of emails from agencies, developers, and companies pitching products or offering opportunities to write about something. Some are relevant to what I cover. Others are general announcements sent to everyone on a mailing list, and then there are follow-ups on conversations I’m already having. I’m sure you get your fair share of these too, even if the subjects are different.

I can’t keep up with all of them, and going through every message to decide whether it deserves a reply is a job in itself. Gmail’s filters help with sorting messages by sender or subject, but the same agency can send me an irrelevant press release and a proposal I actually want to respond to. I need something that reads the message and makes that distinction.

That’s the job I’m giving Tev1. I provide criteria for what deserves a reply, and it checks incoming emails against them. A direct question or a relevant opportunity gets treated differently from a product announcement that doesn’t ask anything of me. I’ve been going back through the emails manually to check its decisions, and so far, it’s been doing the job reliably.

Tev1 4B is a decision model from Together AI. You give it information, a question, and a set of possible answers to choose from. It’s built for tasks like classification and routing, so you can use its answer to decide what happens next in a workflow.

Connecting Tev1 to my email workflow

LM Studio and n8n handle the setup

I’m using n8n for the workflow, with LM Studio serving the model locally. Tev1 uses the /v1/systemone endpoint, where you send the information you want evaluated and the questions it needs to answer.

For Gmail, you can start with n8n’s Gmail Trigger node and connect your account. It checks for new messages at the interval you choose. You then need the sender, subject, and message body available for the next step. Check the node’s output here because its simplified response includes headers and message IDs rather than the full body. You can retrieve the message separately using a Gmail node.

An HTTP Request node sends that information to LM Studio. The email goes in the state field, and the questions field contains the classification instructions. You could define three outcomes — needs a reply, doesn’t need a reply, and needs manual review. Each gets a description explaining which messages belong there. For example, a direct request to confirm availability belongs in the first category, and a general product announcement belongs in the second.

The returned choice gives n8n something to act on. A Switch node can separate those outcomes, and another Gmail node can apply the corresponding label. That gives you a filtered view to open when you’re ready to respond.

The criteria are the part worth spending time on. I’m checking the results against my emails manually because “does this need a reply?” depends on what I’m interested in and which conversations I want to continue. You need to give the model those distinctions.

There are other uses for it

Small decisions across apps and games

Email filtering is one example of what you can do with Tev1. A notification filter is another use I’d like to see, where the model decides whether a message deserves an interruption or can wait. Someone saying they’re outside with your delivery needs your attention sooner than someone sharing a link in a group chat. You’d need an app that can access those notifications and act on the result, but the classification fits what Tev1 does.

This can also work for filtering feeds. You can keep discussions about a game and hide posts containing spoilers, or sort apartment listings according to whether they explicitly allow pets.

There are already some interesting community experiments. Someone has also built a Pac-Man project that compares Tev1 with other models choosing legal moves from the current game state. That’s a more entertaining application than sorting emails, and it opens up ideas for hobby game developers.

A small job worth handing over

I still enjoy trying local models for coding, but I’d like to see more uses like this built into the tools we already use. Finding emails worth replying to is a job I need done every day, and a small model that handles it reliably gives me a good reason to keep it running.

I replaced VS Code's Copilot with a local LLM, and my offline coding got faster

And I am not losing on performance.

item.title: Selling my old PC parts would have been a mistake, so I built a second PC
item.itunes:title: Selling my old PC parts would have been a mistake, so I built a second PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When upgrading or replacing a desktop PC, there's a good chance we have some leftover components. This could include a GPU, CPU, motherboard, RAM, and storage. Sometimes, you may even have a full system ready to go, which is what makes having a second PC available an enticing proposition. Instead of selling these parts for a little side cash, why not consider putting them to good use and putting together a PC for yourself or a loved one? I did the latter, and we've enjoyed countless gaming sessions since.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Why bother building a second PC?

Opening up a world of possibilities!

Putting together a second PC with owned old parts may sound like a wasted opportunity with regard to improving current finances, but there could be scope to save more money down the line. Should one of your components fail and you have nothing to replace it with, the current pricing of PC hardware leaves much to be desired. Having old parts in inventory allows for one to be swapped in should an instance arise where you find yourself scramming for a replacement drive.

The same goes for a motherboard, GPU, or even a power supply. All of these parts cost money to source brand new. If you don't need any more parts in storage, there's the possibility of setting up a home lab or network-attached storage (NAS), and if your old system had a few hard drives, you're already well on your way to creating network storage that can pack a punch. Older PC hardware excels at running Plex, Jellyfin, Immich, Nextcloud, and other services. It could even run some game servers!

Compared to used enterprise gear or running NAS, old PC parts offer solid efficiency, allowing one to undervolt the CPU and take advantage of 16GB of RAM or so. Installing something like Proxmox would enable you to effectively manage the home lab and all running virtual instances, be it Linux containers (LXCs) or virtual machines (VMs). Regardless of what you choose to use old PC hardware for, it'll likely beat the poor resale return. You'll be hard-pressed to recoup what you originally paid outside of memory.

Then there's the possibility to become the next hit streamer. A second system can do a lot more than you may initially realize. For me, I built a system for my wife. We've enjoyed gaming on our Nintendo Switches and mini PC on the TV, but there's something about sitting down for some lengthy sessions behind the larger screen and a PC. That's where the second PC came into action. Utilizing older parts I no longer needed, I could put them to good use, provide the wife with their own machine, and retain all the components.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

A PC build never really comes to an end

It can live on in other ways or forms

My old system didn't really cause any problems. I didn't encounter a CPU issue or anything else of the kind. I simply needed to adjust the platform from the 9950X I had running away. It's a brilliant chip but not the best for gaming. This was when prices were much more reasonable, mind you. I needed a little more gaming performance and more memory for what I threw at the system, and the move seemed like the right call at the time. I have zero regret with that decision, but it meant I left a few parts behind.

I used an old MicroATX board, which was good enough but had a few limitations. I required a new chip and a new board, and so I bought some new RAM too. It also allowed me to consider the CPU cooler, storage, and case to see if there's anything else that warranted changing. For me, it was the cooler (moving from a liquid AIO to an air cooler) and case. That last part was entirely unnecessary. I seem to swap cases more than anything with my personal desktop.

But I managed to put together quite the compelling system with leftover parts. Using the cheapest ITX motherboard I could buy, the AMD Ryzen 9 9950X sits comfortably chugging away as much power as it can. 32GB of DDR4 is installed for all the most demanding games, and the RX 7900 XT is at hand to battle through anything we can throw at it. Honestly, it's a fantastic PC, and one my wife is incredibly happy with. But it's also a solid backup should I ever require it.

Then there's the possibility that she may end up preferring a gaming handheld or laptop at some point, which would free up the entire system for something else. And because it's an ITX-powered PC inside an NZXT H1 (the refreshed model), it could be situated almost anywhere inside the home.

I built a Steam Machine out of spare PC parts and you can, too

item.itunes:title: I finally found an app that makes playing Xbox Game Pass games on Steam Deck a breeze, but it's not perfect
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One key reason I jumped ship from SteamOS and the Steam Deck OLED to the ROG Xbox Ally X is the convenience of accessing a wide variety of games through Xbox Game Pass. Sure, I could install Windows 11 on my Steam Deck OLED, or opt for a complicated dual-boot setup, but I'm a simple guy who prefers simple solutions.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

When I stumbled across Xodus Nexus, an independent, unofficial project that lets you play Xbox Game Pass games on Linux devices like the Steam Deck or Steam Machine, it sounded too good to be true, so I knew I needed to test it out. After a few hours playing several different games, I've concluded it's a surprisingly solid app if you set your expectations appropriately with regard to game compatibility. Also, don't expect the app to magically make the Steam Deck's aging custom AMD Zen 2 APU's any more powerful.

The launcher is built on Xodus with the Nexus backend and Nexus Runtime. It's also not an official project or release from Xodus' development team. At a basic level, Xodus Nexus uses a customized Proton runtime to run Windows PC games on Linux, translating Windows API and DirectX calls into equivalents the operating system can understand.

While Proton also does some of this through Steam, Xodus Nexus goes further by handling Microsoft account authentication and licensing, proprietary Microsoft Store game packages, Xbox runtime APIs, and more. Basically, it fills in the missing pieces required to run Xbox Game Pass titles on SteamOS.

The setup process is very straightforward

I got Xodus Nexus up and running in about 15 minutes

First off, Xodus Nexus is very easy to set up. All you need to do is switch desktop mode on the Steam Deck and download Xodus Nexus version 0.4.1 from GitHub. Next, install the downloaded AppImage with Dolphin File Manager. Once Xodus Nexus is up and running, navigate to Settings and install Nexus Runtime (you need this to play games).

Now, sign in to your Microsoft account to access your PC Game Pass library. This was a bit of a nightmare for me given how complicated my password is, and I ended up connecting my Bluetooth mouse and keyboard to my Steam Deck. You'll need Chrome installed to continue through the authentication process if you have a passkey (I didn't have it installed at first).

Once you're logged in, you'll need to download games just like you would with the Xbox app on a Windows 11 handheld. Thankfully, it supports save-file syncing, including downloading and uploading progress. There's even a useful one-click Add Nexus to Steam option that lets you avoid switching to Desktop Mode to use Xodus Nexus.

It's worth noting that navigating Xodus Nexus on the Steam Deck with its built-in controls can get a little confusing and frustrating. Sometimes the app's UI is completely unresponsive, too. One of the strangest problems I've encountered is that you can't always use the touchscreen to access Game Pass' library.

The little box to select In Game Pass often doesn't open, but for some reason, the Steam Deck's built-in buttons always seem to work. The project is still in the early stages, so future updates will likely iron out UI issues like this.

Asus' ROG Xbox Ally X20 fixes nearly all my issues with the Xbox Ally X, but you probably shouldn't buy it

The OLED screen and design improvements are great — it's just that the Z2 Extreme is showing its age.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Game compatibility and performance are mixed

Some of this comes down to the Steam Deck's lack of power

I quickly realized that not every game works with Xodus Nexus. Still, a lot of notable titles are listed as compatible, including Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons 2, Deep Rock Galactic, No Man's Sky, and Doom: The Dark Ages (you can find a work-in-progress game compatibility list here). Based on what I've researched, the majority of games don't perform quite as well as they do with just straight Proton on Steam and SteamOS, but most titles still run pretty well.

With this in mind, I put Xodus Nexus to the test with a couple of key Game Pass Games. First, I tried Forza Horizon 6, which is listed as compatible, but it barely hits 30fps on Low settings. With FSR 3.1 on, performance improves a bit, but it's still not what I'd call enjoyable and can be downright ugly at times. This is only slightly below the 30-40 FPS Forza Horizon 6 reportedly gets on the Steam Deck through Steam and Proton. It's likely a combination of multiple translation layers and the handheld's aging APU that hinders the performance.

Some games just straight up don't work, either. For example, I tried playing Star Wars: Outlaws, and it wouldn't boot up. Oddly, it also featured a black thumbnail instead of box art. I had the same experience with Far Cry 5, too, which was disappointing, because I've been thinking about revisiting the game. I also couldn't get Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 to load.

On the other hand, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4 ran like an absolute dream on the handheld, hitting a solid 60fps with FSR on and all graphics settings on Medium. Next I played Dredge, a far less resource-intensive game, and it ran at a solid 90fps through Xodus Nexus. I also briefly tried a few other titles, including Gears of War: E-Day, which ran at a pretty solid 30-33fps in my tests (I really didn't expect Gears of War: E-Day to work at all).

I've always preferred SteamOS' pick-up-and-play nature because, unlike the ROG Xbox Ally X or X20, the Steam Deck feels like it was designed to be a gaming device. Despite Microsoft's best efforts with Xbox Mode, the overall Windows 11 handheld experience is still a bit of a mess, whether it's updates that need to be downloaded from several locations, a long boot-up time, or even sleep mode not working consistently.

Thanks to Xodus Nexus, I have a reason to pick up my less powerful, but still very capable Steam Deck OLED. In fact, I've been surprised at how comfortable the Steam Deck OLED is, even compared to the Xbox Ally X20 (it's just been so long since I've held it). With all of this in mind, will I switch back to using the Steam Deck OLED as my main handheld? Probably not, since most new AAA games don't run well on it at this point. On the other hand, if I want to revisit an older title or play an indie game like Dredge, I'll definitely reach for Valve's handheld over my ROG Ally X20.

There's even a useful one-click Add Nexus to Steam option that lets you avoid switching to Desktop Mode to use Xodus Nexus.

It's worth noting that navigating Xodus Nexus on the Steam Deck with its built-in controls can get a little confusing and frustrating. Sometimes the app's UI is completely unresponsive, too. One of the strangest problems I've encountered is that you can't always use the touchscreen to access Game Pass' library.

The little box to select In Game Pass often doesn't open, but for some reason, the Steam Deck's built-in buttons always seem to work. The project is still in the early stages, so future updates will likely iron out UI issues like this.

Game compatibility and performance are mixed

Some of this comes down to the Steam Deck's lack of power

I quickly realized that not every game works with Xodus Nexus. Still, a lot of notable titles are listed as compatible, including Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons 2, Deep Rock Galactic, No Man's Sky, and Doom: The Dark Ages (you can find a work-in-progress game compatibility list here). Based on what I've researched, the majority of games don't perform quite as well as they do with just straight Proton on Steam and SteamOS, but most titles still run pretty well.

With this in mind, I put Xodus Nexus to the test with a couple of key Game Pass Games. First, I tried Forza Horizon 6, which is listed as compatible, but it barely hits 30fps on Low settings. With FSR 3.1 on, performance improves a bit, but it's still not what I'd call enjoyable and can be downright ugly at times. This is only slightly below the 30-40 FPS Forza Horizon 6 reportedly gets on the Steam Deck through Steam and Proton. It's likely a combination of multiple translation layers and the handheld's aging APU that hinders the performance.

Some games just straight up don't work, either. For example, I tried playing Star Wars: Outlaws, and it wouldn't boot up. Oddly, it also featured a black thumbnail instead of box art. I had the same experience with Far Cry 5, too, which was disappointing, because I've been thinking about revisiting the game. I also couldn't get Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 to load.

On the other hand, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4 ran like an absolute dream on the handheld, hitting a solid 60fps with FSR on and all graphics settings on Medium. Next I played Dredge, a far less resource-intensive game, and it ran at a solid 90fps through Xodus Nexus. I also briefly tried a few other titles, including Gears of War: E-Day, which ran at a pretty solid 30-33fps in my tests (I really didn't expect Gears of War: E-Day to work at all).

I've always preferred SteamOS' pick-up-and-play nature because, unlike the ROG Xbox Ally X or X20, the Steam Deck feels like it was designed to be a gaming device. Despite Microsoft's best efforts with Xbox Mode, the overall Windows 11 handheld experience is still a bit of a mess, whether it's updates that need to be downloaded from several locations, a long boot-up time, or even sleep mode not working consistently.

Thanks to Xodus Nexus, I have a reason to pick up my less powerful, but still very capable Steam Deck OLED. In fact, I've been surprised at how comfortable the Steam Deck OLED is, even compared to the Xbox Ally X20 (it's just been so long since I've held it). With all of this in mind, will I switch back to using the Steam Deck OLED as my main handheld? Probably not, since most new AAA games don't run well on it at this point. On the other hand, if I want to revisit an older title or play an indie game like Dredge, I'll definitely reach for Valve's handheld over my ROG Ally X20.

item.itunes:summary:
I stopped viewing 3D printing as a hobbyist's toy around a decade ago, and since then, I've engineered and printed my way out of several challenges posed by store-bought products. It's typically small stuff that leads to greater ease of use or a better quality of life. Six months ago, I bought a new sit-stand frame for my workstation tabletop. In setting it up, I was repeatedly reminded of the significance of 3D-printed bits and bobs.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I found many of these printable models online, which only justified my experience that I wasn't the only one bothered by the subtle quirks of these products. Since I've set it up, I've added a few more 3D-printed bits and bobs, so here are the six most noteworthy additions to my home office, ranging from an IKEA-style diffuser my IKEA work lamp was missing to glow-in-the-dark keyboard wrist rests for more comfortable typing.

A wider foot IKEA Tertial

Ikea really cheaped out on this one's stand

IKEA's Tertial work lamp has been a staple in its catalog since its introduction nearly 30 years ago in 1998. The novel base can clamp the light to a tabletop or mount on a wall with four screws. I needed the repositionability and chose the former, but the constant clamping stress and cantilever load of the lamp created cracks in the plastic base. This also gave it wiggle room to shift out of place.

I earlier wrote about replacing this clamp base with a 3D-printed adapter that converted my car's retired brake rotor into a sturdy stand. However, with the new sit-stand desk, its weight became a major concern, so I printed a replacement for the original IKEA clamp design with a wider foot to stabilize it against shifting, since the larger contact area adds friction and distributes the cantilever load better.

7 practical problems I solved with a 3D printer

My 3D printer has proven itself not just fun, but also a household problem-solver. Here's how

2
By  Jeff Butts

I had to take this road because IKEA refused to replace my cracked lamp foot, and I'm glad I did, because the larger footprint has held the lamp firmly in place since the initial install.

IKEA Tertial lamp diffuser

The essentials I never got

While I'm discussing my IKEA work lamp, I can't skip the missing diffuser. Typically, the Swedish-designed wall and ceiling lamps ship with an integrated diffuser comprising concentric circles. Some of them are adjustable, serving as a dimmer too. My Tertial lamp never got one, and could really benefit from one so the bulb didn't create a spotlight effect.

I found another design online that imitated the brand's iconic diffuser design for printing in white PLA. It's pliable enough to fit inside the hood without disassembly and uses four little protrusions to stay put. This design is the embodiment of the simplicity and ease of use that the 3D printing community has fostered over the years. It looks like a piece of original kit, unless you have a Tertial yourself and know this isn't included. The PLA diffuses the light sufficiently, and though this design isn't adjustable, I've compensated for that with a dimmable smart bulb that seamlessly integrates with my smart home controls and voice assistants.

Wrist rests for typing and mousing around

A lasting solution to wrist strain and carpal tunnel

I spend a majority of my day clacking away at the keyboard and using my mouse. Understandably, I want that to be a comfortable experience. Since switching to a mechanical keyboard, I became acutely aware that they were taller, tilting my wrists upward as I typed. I couldn't hover-type for long, so a wrist rest was inevitable. I started out with a simple plank of wood cut to size, and painted to match.

Eventually, jumping over to my mouse and the transition to split keyboards became two pain points that sent me scurrying to the interwebs in search of a better solution. The DeltaHub Carpio stood out as a classic example that inspired my wrist rest design that moves with your hand so you don't need to lift it off the desk repeatedly. I can just glide over to the mouse and use a split keyboard without issues.

5 ergonomic enhancements you can 3D print for your desk

Improve your posture with these ergonomic prints

By  Sumukh Rao

While my version used PLA bases with swappable TPU cushions for some squishy comfort, I've now moved to another design found online, printed out in glow-in-the-dark PLA. This design is lower profile and better ventilated with the honeycomb pattern, which also helps save filament. All I needed to do was slap a few mouse feet underneath for smooth gliding.

Cable managers

Keep the clutter out of sight, and well organized

I need my workstation to be Zen to get anything productive done, and keeping the cable clutter out of sight was essential to achieve this goal. The sit-stand desk, dual PCs, and a KVM switch for them didn't make matters easy, but 3D printing helped big time. Sure, I used a store-bought cable drag chain and server cable rail to tuck excess lengths and run them to the mid-tower on the floor, but all my wire managers are 3D printed.

I found an effective design that requires inserting or removing each cable at an angle, with enough play to slide through when straight. I printed a few out in PLA for immobile wires under the desk that I'd touch perhaps once in a few months. Then, I used black TPU to string four to five such managers in a row, and mounted them to the desk's edge with 3M VHB tape for daily-use charging cables and such. They've held up just fine for months, and I'm now looking to print one-way cable winders to mount longer charging cords under the desk for an even cleaner look when they're not in use.

Webcam mount

A phone stand just doesn't cut it

My pandemic-era PC build never used a dedicated webcam because I always found them expensive. I'd use my phone instead and enjoy the privacy of webcam-on-demand. I printed several phone stands over the years, because Thingiverse and Printables are full of them, and they only get better. However, a phone stand gave me a ridiculous camera angle staring up at my nostrils, resembling laptops with webcams hidden at keyboard height.

With my display on an arm, I needed to engineer a new solution that moved with the screen, but still gave enough angle adjustment to compensate for screen tilt. I set out to design a universal solution, but found it challenging to account for every monitor thickness and bezel size without ugly screw clamps. While my design eventually worked with just my screen, it can accommodate the thickest of phones.

8 unique 3D prints that I actually use every day

These are the genuinely useful 3D prints that I use the most in my home.

2
By  Adam Conway

The adjustability comes from two bolts with wing nuts I can tighten by hand. Sure, this design could be better, but it wouldn't exist at all without access to desktop 3D printing at a viable price with room for experimentation.

Headphone hanger

Economizing on tabletop space

The final standout in my home office is the headphone hanger I printed off the internet. There are thousands of variations online, but my search parameters were simple. I didn't want to drill the desk; I needed something repositionable that wasn't a tabletop option, with integrated cable management. I finally landed on this design I printed out in grey PETG. It uses a screw clamp design to attach to tabletops of varying thicknesses, and has a secondary grooved hook for excess wire length.

I've used this hanger for my reasonably heavy, fully 3D-printed open-back headphones, and it's held up exceptionally so far. Without this print, I would've paid a lot for a niche product with similar functionality, or a needlessly expensive stand that'd hog valuable space on my desk.

Find a problem to solve

5 things I 3D printed for my home lab that fixed problems I'd been living with

A 3D printer was a surprisingly useful investment for my home lab

3
By  Ayush Pande

A home office is an eclectic mix of small hiccups that snowball into a place you don't find productive. Eliminating small friction and giving everything a clear, designated space is easier than ever with 3D printing. Moreover, if a solution doesn't exist, you can design your own using simple online tools and print refinements or replacement parts as needed.

item.title: I used Claude Code to build an Android app that my family actually uses every day
item.itunes:title: I used Claude Code to build an Android app that my family actually uses every day
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most of my projects with Claude Code are things I want to use myself, whether that’s adding a feature to a self-hosted app or building a tool for a specific task. This time, I wanted to make something for my family. I ended up building a shared grocery list with reminders for things that need to be picked up at a particular time.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

There are already apps for this, of course, but I wanted to try building an Android app around the few features we needed. Everyone gets access to the same list, with quantities, notes, and reminders attached to the items. It’s a fairly modest project, and that’s part of why I picked it.

I gave Claude Code a small brief

A shared list for the family

I started by asking Claude Code to build an Android app where everyone in my family could add groceries to a shared list, specify quantities, and mark items as purchased. I kept the initial brief focused on those actions. I used Opus 5.5 to build the whole thing and hit my five-hour usage limit twice during the process.

The app uses Kotlin and Jetpack Compose for the interface, with Firebase handling sign-in and shared data. I initially considered self-hosting a backend, but there wasn’t much reason to maintain a server for this. The app connects directly to Cloud Firestore, which stores the shopping list and syncs changes across our phones. It also supports offline access, so you can add something without a connection and have it sync once you’re back online.

I went with Firebase’s free Spark plan, which doesn’t require a payment method. For a grocery list shared between a few family members, its free quotas should be enough. Everyone signs in with their Google account, and access rules restrict the list to our family.

A grocery list that only exists on my phone is easy enough to make in a notes app. With this one, anyone can add something when they notice we’re running out, and whoever goes shopping can check the list. Quantities and notes sit alongside each item, so “rice” can include the pack size or brand instead of leaving the person buying it to ask.

I also connected Claude Code to GitHub to keep track of changes. I can ask it to review and commit its work with a clear description, and go back to an earlier version if an update breaks something.

I integrated Google Drive into Claude and my productivity tripled in no time

Beyond copy-paste

By  Parth Shah

Reminders make the list more useful

Remembering what to buy and when

Adding something to a shopping list doesn’t mean I’ll remember to check it before coming home. That’s why I wanted reminders alongside the shared list. I can set a reminder for an item and have the phone notify me around the time I expect to go shopping. The quantity and notes are already in the app, so I don’t have to piece together what I’m supposed to buy from a separate reminder and a message.

These are personal reminders scheduled on the phone. The shopping list is shared with everyone, but setting a reminder for myself doesn’t send a notification to the entire family. Someone else can check the same items and decide when they want to be reminded. I prefer that arrangement to having every addition trigger an alert on everyone’s phone, especially when an item doesn’t need to be bought immediately.

I also kept the reminder system separate from Firebase. Firestore handles the shared data, and Android handles the notification on the device. Once a reminder is scheduled locally, the phone doesn’t need to contact a server at that moment to display it. That keeps this part of the app useful without adding a service whose only job is to send notifications.

I’m keeping remotely assigned reminders out of this version. Having someone create a reminder on my phone without me opening the app would require push delivery and additional backend logic. For now, I can open the family list, see what we need, and set my own reminder before heading out.

item.itunes:summary:
I love Obsidian for its flexibility, customization options, and the freedom to build a knowledge management system exactly how I want. However, maintaining a well-organized vault is a different story. As my collection of notes grew, I found myself spending more time moving files between folders, fixing misplaced notes, and keeping everything tidy than actually writing.

That’s when I found a free community plugin that changed how I manage my vault: AutoMover. With a few simple rules, I managed to automate the entire organization process.

I tried replacing Notion with Obsidian as my main note-taking app and here’s how it went

The truth about switching from Notion to Obsidian

7
By  Parth Shah

What is AutoMover, and how does it work?

A simple solution to vault chaos

AutoMover is a free, open-source Obsidian community plugin that does exactly what its name suggests. It automatically moves notes and files into designated folders based on rules I define. Instead of manually sorting my notes every time I create something new, I can simply tell the plugin what to look for and where to move matching files.

Getting started is straightforward. I opened Obsidian’s settings, headed to Community plugins, searched for AutoMover, and installed it. Once enabled, the plugin gave me several ways to organize my vault, including filename patterns, tags, and project properties. It even supports regular expressions for more advanced automation rules.

The real magic lies in how these rules execute. I can configure AutoMover to organize notes when I open them, trigger the process manually, or run it on a schedule. There are also exclusion rules to protect important folders and files from unwanted changes.

Unlike complicated automation tools, AutoMover doesn’t require coding knowledge or external services. Everything happens within Obsidian, and I remain in complete control of how my vault is organized.

Creating my first automation rule

My notes finally find their homes

The first thing I did after installing AutoMover was create a handful of filename-based rules. I headed to the plugin’s settings, entered a keyword under the search criteria, and assigned a destination folder.

For example, I created a rule that looks for the word ‘Voyage’ in filenames and automatically moves matching notes into my Personal/Travel folders. Similarly, I configured rules for ‘Article’ and ‘Meeting’ to send relevant notes into their respective folders under Work.

Previously, I had to manually select the relevant folder every time I created a new note. Now, I can create notes in my inbox and let AutoMover handle the sorting when its rules run. It’s a straightforward setup that saves me from repetitive housekeeping.

Filename-based automation works well, but I don’t always want to follow a strict naming convention. That’s where AutoMover’s tag rules come into play. Instead of relying on specific words in a note’s title, I can assign a tag and let the plugin determine its destination.

For example, when I come across an interesting productivity trick or a potential topic for an upcoming article, I create a quick note with a descriptive title and add the #ideas tag. I have set AutoMover to move matching notes into my Ideas folder.

The clever part is that I can use filenames and tags together. AutoMover prioritizes filename-based rules over tag rules, so notes with matching titles follow those rules first.

My vault now cleans itself automatically

I no longer schedule cleanup sessions

Instead of manually triggering the plugin every time I create a new note, I configured it to run automatically at five-minute intervals. Now, whenever I am working in Obsidian, AutoMover periodically scans my vault, checks notes against my predefined rules, and moves matching files to their set folders.

Now, I can spend an afternoon brainstorming article ideas, creating research notes, and documenting personal projects without worrying about folder management. As long as Obsidian is running, AutoMover handles the boring part.

Previously, I would occasionally dedicate time to cleaning up my inbox and moving misplaced notes. This routine has practically disappeared.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

Exclusion rules prevent unwanted changes

Some notes should never move

While I love the convenience of automatic organization, I don’t want AutoMover to mess with every corner of my vault. I have certain folders, such as Templates, Dashboards, and Archives, where everything is already arranged exactly how I want. The last thing I need is an automation rule accidentally moving an important file and affecting my workflow.

Thankfully, AutoMover offers exclusion rules to prevent such situations. I can specify which files or folders should remain untouched, even if they match my existing filename or tag-based rules.

For instance, I can protect my Templates folder so that a meeting note template doesn’t suddenly end up in my Work/Meetings folder.

A smarter vault without the maintenance

A well-organized Obsidian vault shouldn’t require constant attention, and AutoMover proves exactly that. Instead of wasting time deciding where each note belongs, I can focus on capturing ideas, working on projects, and connecting information.

AutoMover handles the housekeeping with little intervention. Of course, it takes some initial effort to configure the right rules, but the long-term convenience easily makes up for it.

If you have been struggling to keep your Obsidian vault under control, I highly recommend giving AutoMover a shot.
